newsitem.title: TANZANIA: UN investigates Rwanda genocide tribunal.
newsitem.headline: UN investigates Rwanda genocide tribunal.

text.p: A U.N. official investigated the tribunal on Rwanda's 1994 genocide on Wednesday amid charges that the slow-moving judicial process has been paralysed by its own staff.

Speaking on the eve of the resumption of a trial of a Rwandan accused of genocide, the information chief for the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda accused Acting Administration Chief George Anderson, a Liberian, of obstructing activity.

"Things have been paralysed by the acting chief of administration. The investigation is ongoing," said Beatrice Lacoste, confirming an investigator from the U.N. inspector general's office had arrived at the tribunal's headquarters in Arusha.
"Yes, we've had problems at the tribunal," Lacoste told Reuters. "There's no question there are problems in administration. More red tape than there should be."
She said the tribunal suffered from a lack of publicity for trials leading to a poor image, problems over getting equipment that caused delays and administrative problems.
Tribunal staff have complained in the past about incompetence among fellow staff, U.N. politics and bureaucracy.

The trial resumes on Thursday of Jean Paul Akayesu, 43, who has pleaded not guilty to charges of crimes against humanity and genocide during the killing of up to a million Rwandan Tutsis and their Hutu supporters in 1994. A lawyer for Akayesu said he would seek a seven-month postponement.

The tribunal, with a budget of $36 million this year, indicted 21 suspects of whom 12 are in custody. Judges had hoped trials in this northern Tanzanian farming town would show mass killings would not go unpunished.
But the start in earnest of the first trial on Thursday has been overshadowed by new ethnic conflict in eastern Zaire uprooting more than 500,000 Rwandan Hutu and Burundian refugees.

Karl Paschke, a German diplomat who serves as U.N. inspector general, hinted at the investigation in a report in New York on Tuesday that focused on problems in procurement and planning in U.N. peacekeeping ventures.

U.N. sources said Paschke, U.N. undersecretary-general for internal oversight services, had sent an investigator to Arusha to look into staff allegations of victimisation, delays in procuring equipment and obstruction of efforts to publicise the trials.
In his report, Paschke said the tribunal had hired staff, including interpreters and translators, who lacked expertise.

The New York Times said several staff and legal experts on loan to the tribunal from European and other nations claimed the acting chief of administration was slowing if not sabotaging the work of legal officials.
Non-African employees and experts attached to the tribunal contend they have been singled out for criticism in a campaign to drive them out of jobs, the newspaper said.
On Tuesday, another Rwandan appeared in a tribunal courtroom. Obed Ruzindana pleaded not guilty to conspiracy to commit genocide, crimes against humanity and violation of the Geneva Conventions.
The court ruled he would next appear on February 20.
Ruzindana was arrested on September 20 by Kenyan police and transferred to Arusha two days later. He is one of four accused held in Arusha, including one at a hospital.
